title: Rice Hispa: White Streaks, Burnt Looking Fields and Control
metaTitle: Rice Hispa: White Leaf Streaks, Damage and Control
metaDescription: Rice hispa beetles scrape rice leaves into white streaks and the grubs mine them. Learn the signs, how to tell it apart and how to manage it.
excerpt: Rice hispa is a small spiny beetle that scrapes the green tissue of rice leaves. The leaves show white streaks and turn papery, and heavy attacks make a field look burnt. This page shows how to spot rice hispa and how to keep it low without wasteful spraying.

blocks.text:
Rice hispa (Dicladispa armigera) is a leaf beetle. The adults scrape the upper surface of the leaf blade and leave only the lower skin. The grubs tunnel between the two skins of the leaf and make irregular, translucent patches.

EPPO lists the beetle as present in the Philippines, without details on how common it is. It is also listed in many other rice countries in Asia. So it is worth knowing, because a bad attack looks like a burnt field.

blocks.caption: Quick facts
rows: In the vegetative stage, more in the rainy season and in crowded, heavily fertilized fields.
Adult beetles scrape the leaf surface, and the grubs mine inside the leaf between its two skins.

blocks.text: Hold up a damaged leaf to the light. White streaks running parallel to the midrib are the adult feeding. Irregular, translucent white patches that follow the leaf veins are the grub mines. Look for the small spiny beetles on the leaves. White patches on the inner leaf margins of unopened leaves point to the [rice whorl maggot](/pests/rice-whorl-maggot) instead.

items: White streaks run along the leaf, parallel to the midrib.
Irregular translucent patches follow the leaf veins where grubs mined.
Damaged leaves turn whitish and papery, and wither.
Heavy attacks make whole patches of the field look burnt.
Plants are less vigorous when the damage is severe.

blocks.title: Do not confuse it with
blocks.text: Wind tears, the [rice leaffolder](/pests/rice-leaffolder) and the whorl maggot all leave pale marks. Hispa leaves streaks along the leaf and spiny beetles on it.
How Rice Hispa Hurts Your Palay

IRRI says that when damage is severe, plants become less vigorous. The sources we read give no percent yield loss and no action threshold, so we state none. The best guide is your own field. Check the leaves each week in the vegetative stage and note how many hills show fresh streaks.

items: Avoid over fertilizing, because heavily fertilized fields favor the beetle.
Do not plant too close. Wide spacing keeps the leaf density low, and dense leaves favor hispa.
Remove grassy weeds in the field and along the bunds, because they are alternate hosts.
Walk the field in the vegetative stage and look for the beetles and the white streaks.
Protect the natural enemies. Small wasps attack the eggs and grubs, reduviid bugs attack the adults, and three fungi infect them. See the guide on [rice insects](/pests/rice-insects).

blocks.text: The sources we read name no insecticide for rice hispa in the Philippines, so we list no ingredient. EPPO gives no detail on how common the beetle is here. Ask a PhilRice or DA technician before you spray anything. Early sprays also kill the spiders and wasps that protect the crop.

blocks.title: Spray safely
blocks.text: Use only products registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label for the rate, the timing and the protective clothing. Switch to a different insecticide group next time, so the pest does not learn to survive it. Our [guide to integrated pest management](/pests/integrated-pest-management) explains how.

items: Keep the bunds and canals free of grassy weeds.
Use the recommended spacing and fertilizer rate.
Avoid sprays in the first 30 to 40 days after transplanting unless there is a true outbreak.
Report an unusual outbreak to your municipal agriculture office.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Rice Hispa

items.q: Is rice hispa common in the Philippines?
items.a: EPPO lists it as present in the Philippines, but gives no detail on how common it is here.

items.q: What does hispa damage look like?
items.a: White streaks along the leaf from the adults, and translucent patches from the grubs. Severe damage makes the field look burnt.

items.q: How do I keep it away?
items.a: Avoid over fertilizing and close spacing, and remove grassy weeds. These are the steps IRRI lists.
